title: Design Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: a dynamic array simulation versus a true doubly linked list with dummy sentinels and closer-end index walking.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a linked list, supporting: get(index) (return the value at index, or -1 if invalid), addAtHead(val), addAtTail(val), addAtIndex(index, val) (insert before the index-th node, or at the end if index equals the length, doing nothing if index is greater), and deleteAtIndex(index) (delete the index-th node, if valid).

blocks.caption: A doubly linked list with dummy head/tail sentinels and a running size counter supports every operation efficiently

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of operations (get, addAtHead, addAtTail, addAtIndex, deleteAtIndex), each with its own arguments"],["Output","For each get call, the value at that index (or -1 if invalid); other operations produce no direct output"],["Goal","Support all 5 operations efficiently, ideally O(1) for head/tail operations and O(n) (but with a small constant) for arbitrary-index operations"],["Constraints","0 <= index, val <= 1000; at most 2000 calls will be made to get, addAtHead, addAtTail, addAtIndex, and deleteAtIndex"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Need to support insertion/deletion at ARBITRARY positions efficiently","A doubly linked list, since it allows O(1) insertion/deletion once positioned at the right node (unlike an array, which needs an O(n) shift)"],["Both head and tail operations should be fast, and access can start from EITHER end","Dummy head AND tail sentinel nodes, plus a size counter to decide which end is closer to any given index"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

This is a "design" problem: instead of solving one specific computation, a data structure must be built from scratch that correctly supports several different operations, matching the exact semantics of a real linked list.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building Your Own Line of People With Read/Insert/Remove Rules
blocks.text: Like building a system to manage a line of people from scratch, where you need to support: "who is at position i?", "add someone to the very front," "add someone to the very back," "insert someone at an arbitrary position," and "remove the person at an arbitrary position." Keeping track of both ends of the line (not just the front) lets requests near the back be handled just as quickly as requests near the front, by simply starting the walk from whichever end is closer.

blocks.caption: Dummy sentinels at both ends let every operation start its walk from whichever side is closer to the target index

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: addAtHead(1), addAtTail(3), addAtIndex(1,2), get(1), deleteAtIndex(1), get(1)
5. How Should We Think?

Before using a plain array (whose insertions/deletions in the middle cost O(n) due to shifting), notice that a doubly linked list with sentinel nodes at both ends directly supports every required operation, letting access start from whichever end is closer to the target index.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: addAtHead and addAtTail are naturally O(1) on a doubly linked list, since both ends are directly reachable via sentinel nodes, with no shifting required.

Observation 2: get(index), addAtIndex(index, val), and deleteAtIndex(index) all first require WALKING to the correct node, which costs O(index) or O(size - index) depending on which end the walk starts from.

Observation 3: Maintaining a running size counter allows choosing, for ANY index, whichever end (head or tail) is closer, roughly halving the average walk distance compared to always starting from the head.

Observation 4: Using DUMMY sentinel nodes for both the head and tail (rather than tracking real head/tail node references directly) elegantly avoids needing special-case logic for empty-list or boundary insertions/deletions, since every real node always has a genuine (possibly dummy) node on both sides.

Recognizing that a doubly linked list with sentinels directly mirrors the operations this problem asks for is the key design insight.
This is a doubly linked list with dummy head and tail sentinels, plus a size counter, choosing the closer end to start each indexed walk from.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a plain dynamic array (like a Python list or Java ArrayList) to simulate the linked list's values directly, relying on the array's own built-in insert/remove-at-index operations.
Step by step algorithm

items: get(index): directly index into the array (with bounds checking).
addAtHead/addAtTail/addAtIndex: use the array's built-in insert operation at the appropriate position.
deleteAtIndex: use the array's built-in remove operation at the given position (with bounds checking).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Delegating to the array's built-in insert/remove operations keeps the code very short, at the cost of an O(n) shift on every insertion or deletion not at the very end.
get(index) is naturally O(1) on an array, unlike on an actual linked list, which is the main advantage this brute force has, at the expense of slow inserts/deletes.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly implements every required operation's semantics, since the array's built-in operations behave exactly as specified.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: get is O(1); addAtHead, addAtIndex, and deleteAtIndex are O(n) in the worst case, due to shifting all subsequent elements.
Space: O(n) for the underlying array.

Limitation: while simple, this does not actually implement a "linked list" in spirit (get should typically be the SLOW operation, and insert/delete should be fast once positioned); a true doubly linked list with sentinels matches the intended data structure more faithfully, and can start indexed walks from whichever end is closer.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses an array, where get is fast but insert/delete are slow (shifting). Instead, build an actual doubly linked list with a dummy head sentinel and a dummy tail sentinel, plus a running size counter. For any index-based operation, walk from whichever sentinel (head or tail) is closer to that index, based on comparing the index to size/2. Insertion and deletion, once positioned at the correct node, are then simple O(1) pointer re-links.

Maintain head and tail dummy sentinels, connected to each other when empty, and a size counter. A helper nodeAt(index) walks from head.next forward if index < size/2, or from tail.prev backward otherwise. addAtHead/addAtTail directly insert before head.next/tail respectively (O(1)). addAtIndex walks to (or past, for the very end) the correct position and inserts before it. deleteAtIndex walks to the correct node and unlinks it.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a doubly linked list with dummy head/tail sentinels and a size counter, always starting indexed walks from whichever end is closer.
Dry run for addAtHead(1), addAtTail(3), addAtIndex(1,2), get(1)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: get(1) correctly returns 2, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: addAtHead/addAtTail are O(1); get, addAtIndex, and deleteAtIndex are O(min(index, size - index)), roughly halving the average walk distance compared to always starting from one end.
Space: O(n) for the n real nodes, plus O(1) fixed overhead for the two sentinels.
Why This Works

The dummy sentinels guarantee that EVERY real node (and even an empty list's "virtual" boundary) always has a genuine node on both sides, eliminating null-pointer special cases entirely from the insertion and deletion logic. Choosing which end to walk from based on comparing the index to size/2 never changes the CORRECTNESS of the result, only how quickly that correct node is reached.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["index closer to the front (index < size/2)","Walk forward from head.next"],["index closer to the back (index >= size/2)","Walk backward from tail.prev"],["addAtIndex with index == size (insert at the very end)","Insert directly before the tail sentinel, avoiding an unnecessary walk"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The two sentinels are linked to each other in the constructor, correctly representing an empty list without any real nodes.

insertBefore(node, val) is a single shared helper used by addAtHead, addAtTail, and addAtIndex, since inserting before a target node is exactly the same operation regardless of which "logical" operation triggered it.
nodeAt(index) is the only place that needs to decide which end to walk from, keeping that logic centralized and reused by get, addAtIndex, and deleteAtIndex.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Designing a custom linked list from scratch is best served by dummy sentinel nodes at BOTH ends (avoiding null-pointer special cases entirely) combined with a size counter that lets every indexed operation start its walk from whichever end is closer.
Common mistakes

items: Not using sentinel nodes, leading to awkward special-case handling for empty-list operations or head/tail insertions and deletions.
Always walking from the head regardless of the target index, missing the "start from the closer end" optimization that roughly halves average walk distance.
Off-by-one errors in addAtIndex, particularly the boundary case where index equals the current size (insert at the very end).

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["get on an empty list, or any out-of-range index","Returns -1"],["addAtIndex with index equal to the current size","Inserts at the very end, equivalent to addAtTail"],["addAtIndex with a negative index, or greater than size","Treated as index 0 (if negative) or ignored (if greater than size), per the problem's specification"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly justifying the choice of dummy sentinels at BOTH ends (not just one) up front demonstrates awareness of exactly which edge cases they eliminate.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a linked list from scratch, supporting get/insert/delete at arbitrary positions" points toward a doubly linked list with dummy sentinels at both ends and a size counter for closer-end selection.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why use a DOUBLY (not singly) linked list here? Deletion at an arbitrary index needs access to the node's PREVIOUS neighbor to re-link around it; a singly linked list would require an extra walk just to find that previous node.

How much does the "start from the closer end" optimization actually help? It roughly halves the WORST-CASE and average walk distance (from O(n) to O(n/2)), though the asymptotic complexity class remains O(n) either way.

How would you extend this design to support an O(1) getFirst/getLast? Simply reading head.next.val or tail.prev.val directly gives O(1) access to both ends, already implicit in the current sentinel design.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A "design"-style problem applying the same doubly linked list mechanics (insertion, deletion, sentinel nodes) used implicitly throughout this category, now made fully explicit as the deliverable itself.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: get O(1), insert/delete O(n) time; O(n) space.
Optimized (doubly linked list with sentinels): all operations O(min(index, size - index)) time; O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Doubly linked list with dummy head/tail sentinels and a size counter
Core Idea: Sentinels eliminate null-pointer special cases entirely; the size counter lets every indexed walk start from whichever end (head or tail) is closer
Time: O(1) for head/tail operations; O(min(index, size - index)) for arbitrary-index operations
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Choosing the closer end to walk from never changes correctness, only how quickly the target node is reached
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Dummy head <-> ... <-> dummy tail; walk from whichever end is closer, based on comparing index to size/2
